87.0.0.en: 1- His foundation is in the holy mountains.

87.0.1.en: 1- The foundation of God He laid in the holy mountains on which the city of Jerusalem was built, and in which the temple of God was built by the hand of Solomon. God's foundation is faith in Him, or His teachings, or it is Christ Himself, the foundation on which the building of His Church stands, or on which the life of His children who believe in Him stands. The mountains are holy because God sanctified them by dwelling in His temple, and the foundation in the New Testament is also the teaching of the Apostles, and their successors the bishops and priests, and all the servants.

87.0.2.en: 2- Mountains signify steadfastness, and also loftiness and elevation above material things, and on them the temple was built. And the Church of the New Testament is steadfast in Christ and lifted above the world.

87.1.0.en: 2- The Lord loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.

87.1.1.en: 1- The gates of Zion are the gates of the temple, and God loved them more than all the gates and dwellings of Jacob, that is, the dwellings of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, because the kingdom of Judah, in which the city of Jerusalem and its temple lie, was the one that continued to worship God. As for the ten tribes, they worshiped idols after they split and separated, after the reign of Solomon, under Jeroboam the son of Nebat. So God loved Jerusalem because He dwelt in its temple and rejoiced in the worship of His children offered in it. And in Jerusalem godly kings appeared, such as David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah, who led their people in the worship of God.

87.1.2.en: 2- The gates of Zion are the Church, which God loved because He founded her with His blood on the Cross, and she is better than all the dwellings of the world, and the gates of Zion are also the Christian virtues.

87.2.0.en: 3- Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah.

87.2.1.en: 1- The glories of the city of God spring from the temple of God that is in it, in which He dwells by His Holy Spirit, blessing the place and everyone who comes to it to worship God.

87.2.2.en: 2- The city of God is the Church, and her glories are Christ, who gives His Body and Blood to His children, and likewise the angels and saints who fill her, for the Church is the house of the angels and the place of the saints, and she is also the heavenly Jerusalem whose glory cannot be expressed.

87.2.3.en: 3- The city of God is also the Virgin Mary, whom the Holy Spirit sanctified, and in whom Christ was born, and to whom God gave many glories which the Midnight Praise expresses in various forms every day in the Theotokia.

87.2.4.en: 4- This passage ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical tone that gives the chanter and the hearer an opportunity to meditate on the greatness of the Church, in which God dwells by His Spirit, with His angels and saints around Him.

87.2.5.en: If Jerusalem is holy through its temple, and is a symbol of the Church and of the Virgin, then it is also a symbol of your soul, my brother, in which God has dwelt by His Holy Spirit. If God loves your soul and prefers it to many souls, it is because He dwells in it. And the more you respond to His dwelling by prayer and meditation, He rejoices in you, works in you, and fills you with many blessings.

87.3.s.en: (2) Jerusalem, the salvation and joy of the Gentiles

87.3.0.en: 4- “I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me: behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there.”

87.3.1.en: Rahab: a word meaning pride, and what is meant by it is Egypt.

87.3.2.en: Tyre: a city on the northern coast of the Mediterranean, and it was the greatest commercial city in ancient times, and was distinguished by wealth.

87.3.4.en: The Psalm shows the different peoples of the world at that time, namely Babylon, which became an empire, and Egypt, which was a great empire, and likewise Philistia with its five cities lying on the coast of the Mediterranean, and Tyre, the most important commercial city in the world at that time, and Cush, distinguished by the strength of its men in war. What is meant is that the different countries of the world, with all their distinctions, are where faith in Christ was born, and churches were established in them, and they followed Christ and left their idols and sins. This is the new Jerusalem, the Church of the New Testament, and she is what is meant by the phrase “this man was born there.” So God mentioned all these countries, that is, all the Gentiles in addition to the Jewish people, and in the fullness of time He became incarnate and redeemed them, and gave them salvation, and established His Church everywhere.

87.4.0.en: 5- And of Zion it shall be said, “This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her.”

87.4.1.en: The Psalm speaks about Jerusalem, the city of God, and calls it Zion, which is the most important of the mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built, so the name Zion is applied to the city of Jerusalem. This Psalm speaks to her, and says to her that many sons will be born in her one after another, for God the Most High has established her, so birth in her continues. What is meant by Zion is the Church, in which many sons will be born through the baptismal font, and become Christians who live for ever with God in the heavenly Jerusalem.

87.5.0.en: 6- The Lord shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah.

87.5.1.en: 1- The Lord counts, as one who writes the names of His children in the Book of Life, and He writes the names of those who believe in Him from the peoples, that is, the Gentiles who were born in Baptism and became Christians.

87.5.2.en: 2- The Lord Jesus Christ was enrolled and counted in the books of the peoples through Caesar Augustus in Bethlehem.

87.5.3.en: 3- “This man was born there” means Jesus Christ our Lord, who was born in Bethlehem.

87.5.4.en: 4- This verse ends with the word “Selah,” a musical tone for meditating on the humility of Christ in being born as a man, and His greatness in His love for mankind.

87.6.0.en: 7- As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee.

87.6.1.en: 1- All the worshipers who chant in Jerusalem rejoice, accompanied by musical instruments, and this happened in the days of David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah, and there was great joy in the city.

87.6.2.en: 2- In the Church all her members sing hymns of thanksgiving and praise to God after receiving the Body and Blood of the Lord, for they have become one in Christ, gathered by one love.

87.6.3.en: 3- In the heavenly Jerusalem they sing great hymns, as if they were playing musical instruments in unspeakable joy, in which all the heavenly ones share.

87.6.4.en: The greatest place in the world is the Church, where Christ dwells by His Holy Spirit and His most holy Body and Blood. So do not be slow to take part in her, that you may be united with Christ and rejoice, and then go out to rejoice and call everyone to enjoy it with you.

87.6.5.en: Pains and supplications. A song of praise. A Psalm for the sons of Korah. To the chief musician, upon the lute, for singing. A poem of Heman the Ezrahite. “O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee ...” (v. 1). Introduction:

87.6.7.en: Heman the Ezrahite, who was one of the three chief singers, and used to stand at the right hand of Asaph the chief. He was of the clan of Zerah the son of Judah, that is, of the tribe of Judah, and he was counted among the prominent wise men after King Solomon (1 Kgs 4:31).

87.6.8.en: 2- This Psalm shows severe pains that the writer suffered, yet he still prays even though he feels no consolation, but his hope is in God. It is a personal lament resembling the laments of Job and Jeremiah.

87.6.9.en: 3- This is the only Psalm that goes through sufferings to its end, and does not announce, even at its close, God's intervention and the solution of the problem.

87.6.10.en: 4- This Psalm is considered a prophecy about the sufferings of Christ on the Cross.

87.6.11.en: 5- This Psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya, and it suits every person who suffers pains, and calls him to continue in prayer and not despair however great his sufferings.

87.6.12.en: 6- This Psalm gives reasons for the petitions it makes to God, to stress the importance of its petition, and this is in the verses (vv. 1, 2, 3, 7, 12, 17).

88.0.0.en: 1- O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee:

88.0.1.en: The writer of the Psalm feels severe distress, so that he cries out all day, by day and by night, because the pain is continual. But at the same time he has hope in God his Savior, and indeed he has no salvation except in Him, so he says “God of my salvation,” that is, the only One responsible for his salvation.

88.1.0.en: 2- Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;

88.1.1.en: 1- Heman pleads with God that his prayer reach Him, that is, that He take care to hear his prayer, and also his cry, which may be inward, heard by no one, but a strong and painful groaning within his soul. He trusts that God is a compassionate Father who will care for him and rescue him from his troubles. And the inclining of the ear means great humility on God's part, and a special care that supports Heman and encourages him to bear the sufferings. For the feeling of God's presence within the affliction is very consoling and comforting.

88.1.2.en: 2- These two verses (vv. 1, 2) are a prophecy of the cries of Christ and His sufferings on the Cross, which He expressed by His saying, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46).

88.2.0.en: 3- For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave.

88.2.2.en: The writer of the Psalm expresses his sufferings, saying that they are so many that his soul is full of them, like one who eats food and is filled and cannot eat any more; so his soul cannot bear other calamities. And he also feels that he has come near to death (the grave), and almost loses his hope of deliverance from the sufferings.

88.3.0.en: 4- I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength:

88.3.1.en: The pit: a deep, wide hole.

88.3.2.en: 1- He feels that he is about to die, thrown into a pit whose bottom he does not know, and he also feels that he has lost all strength to resist the sufferings, because they are so severe. Perhaps he remembers Joseph the righteous, who after bearing the sufferings of slavery in the house of Potiphar was cast into prison, after he had endured being thrown into the pit by his brothers, who wanted to kill him, while he had no strength.

88.3.3.en: 2- These verses also (vv. 3, 4) and those that follow are prophecies about the sufferings of Christ on the Cross.

88.4.0.en: 5- Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand.

88.4.1.en: 1- From the severity of the pain the writer of the Psalm felt that he was near death, as if he had already reached the grave, and his bed, or resting place, was there among the slain, and he no longer enjoyed God's care and attention, that is, he felt forgotten and abandoned by God, and this is a very hard feeling, for he is suffering not only physically but even more psychologically.

88.4.2.en: 2- All these sufferings are a prophecy of what Christ felt on the Cross, as He was approaching the tomb to lie there, like those who sleep and the slain, forgotten by God, so that He felt that God had forsaken Him.

88.5.0.en: 6- Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps.

88.5.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm feels that God has put him in the depths of a great and deep pit, where the darkness is intense. All this expresses his hard sufferings, so that despair almost closes in on him.

88.5.2.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ on the Cross, for He feels that He is nearing death to go down to the depths of Hades, but to save His children and bring them up from it, and not to remain in it.

88.6.0.en: 7- Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah.

88.6.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm felt that the sufferings were severe as a result of the wrath of God that lay upon him, that is, became fixed and settled, as if he were in the depths of the sea, covered with water and its currents, until he became utterly abased. And God allowed all this so that he might be humbled, repent and be purified.

88.6.2.en: 2- This verse also shows how Christ bore the sins of the whole world, and endured the divine wrath that ought to have come upon man, so Christ bore it for him, and likewise on the Cross, to redeem mankind.

88.6.3.en: 3- The verse ends with the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditating on the extent of Christ's suffering of pains for us to redeem us, that we may repent of our sins and offer Him constant thanks.

88.7.0.en: 8- Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth.

88.7.1.en: An abomination: filthy and unclean, and what is meant here is that he became a shame.

88.7.2.en: 1- The psychological distress of this speaker increased as his loved ones and friends kept away from him, for they saw him as a shame and did not want to come near him, and this shame closed in on him with the psychological pains it carries, and he cannot come out of them. And this represents the extreme of psychological pain.

88.7.3.en: 2- This is what happened to Christ when everyone left Him at the Cross, and thought Him an evildoer deserving death, and thus He suffered psychological pains, and not only physical ones, in addition to spiritual pains, for He bore the sins of the whole world, and He cannot come out of these pains because He wants to complete the redemption.

88.8.0.en: 9- Mine eye mourneth by reason of affliction: Lord, I have called daily upon thee, I have stretched out my hands unto thee.

88.8.1.en: 1- The eye of this sufferer also grew weak from the severity of the humiliation that came upon him, but he continued to call on God and did not lose his hope, so he continued in his prayer, stretching out his hands, asking for the help of God, who still loves him and whom he calls upon.

88.8.2.en: 2- Likewise Christ, from the severity of the pains, showed humiliation in the look of His eyes, because He bore all the sins of the world, but He remained with His hands stretched out on the Cross, praying and calling on the Father with many words.

88.8.3.en: When your sufferings increase, lift your heart in prayer to God, and trust that He hears you and rewards you, and turns that into glory, and blesses your life.

88.9.0.en: 10- Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. 11- Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? 12- Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

88.9.1.en: 1- Since the writer of the Psalm felt that he had come near to death, he said to God: why do You not rescue me from these pains and from that death? For after death a man cannot worship You, nor can the shades, that is, the souls that have fallen asleep, do anything, nor do the graves hear any glorification of God or proclamation of the truth. And from the dark grave or the dead who have left life there comes no magnifying of God.

88.9.2.en: 2- The grave and the darkness signify the death of sin, for whoever is immersed in sin cannot glorify God.

88.9.3.en: 3- The only person who was able to glorify God while in the tomb is Christ, because He was able to do the greatest wonder, which is the Resurrection.

88.9.4.en: 4- He ends the tenth verse with the word “Selah,” which is an invitation to meditate on what comes after death.

88.9.5.en: Do not lose your hope in your Christ however much troubles increase upon you, for He is able to bring life out of death, and to bring out of affliction many blessings that gladden your heart and fill you with happiness.

88.9.6.en: [3] The prayer of one who meditates (vv. 13 - 18):

88.10.0.en: 13- But unto thee have I cried, O Lord; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee.

88.10.1.en: The early morning (al-ghadat): the early morning. Despite all the pains the writer of the Psalm suffers, he continued in his prayers, and from the beginning of the day, in the early morning, he offered many prayers before God, and expressed his cry as if God were walking in a procession while he offers these prayers and cries to Him, that He may rescue him from his troubles. He presses God and awaits His answer, that is, his hope is still firm in God.

88.11.0.en: 14- Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?

88.11.1.en: From the severity of the writer's suffering, and God's not intervening to lift the pains from him, he reproaches God with the boldness of love and hope, because He is slow to rescue him, and says to Him that Your silence means Your rejection, and the turning away of Your face from me despite my great need, that is, he asks that God intervene quickly.

88.12.0.en: 15- I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted. 16- Thy fierce wrath goeth over me; thy terrors have cut me off. 17- They came round about me daily like water; they compassed me about together. 18- Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness. Thy terrors: great calamities.

88.12.1.en: Thy fierce wrath: your intense anger.

88.12.2.en: They compassed me about: surrounded me on every side.

88.12.3.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm continues his reproach of God with boldness and hope, saying to Him: You know the extent of my suffering since my youth. I am poor and weak and resigned to the afflictions and pains that You permit. Indeed, O Lord, You allowed me great afflictions when You were angry with me. He likens the afflictions to the waters of the sea into which he fell, and which surrounded him on every side, and he became unable to come out of them, and they continued all day, that is, all his life, and all his loved ones were scattered from him, and he lived in the darkness of affliction.

88.12.4.en: 2- These verses are prophecies about the sufferings of Christ and His affliction on the Cross, as we explained before in the preceding verses.

88.12.5.en: When you enter into afflictions and suffer much, know that this is by God's permission, that you may feel for those who suffer, and as God brought you out of the affliction, help others with all you can to lift their sufferings from them.

88.12.6.en: The mercies of God and His promises. A poem of Ethan the Ezrahite. “I will sing of the mercies of the Lord for ever ...” (v. 1). Introduction

88.12.7.en: 1- Its writer: Ethan the Ezrahite, who was one of the three chief singers in the days of King David. He used to stand at the left hand of Asaph, the highest chief of the singers, while Heman the Ezrahite used to stand at the right hand of Asaph, in the great religious celebrations. And Ethan was chief of six companies of singers, and his six sons were chiefs over these companies (1 Chr 25).

88.12.8.en: 2- This Psalm is a prophecy about the condition of the people of God during the captivity, when they were exposed to attack by enemies, and the humiliation of the king, the rulers and the people.

88.12.9.en: The writer of the Psalm may be from the descendants of Ethan the Ezrahite, and wrote it in the days of the captivity.

88.12.10.en: 3- This Psalm is different from the other Psalms, because they begin by crying out to God and asking for His mercies, and end with thanksgiving and praise. But this Psalm begins with thanksgiving, then asks for the mercies of God, and this is the thought of the Church to this day, for she begins all her liturgical prayers with thanksgiving, then asks for what she needs, to teach us that our spontaneous prayers should be in the same manner.

88.12.11.en: 4- This Psalm is the last in the third book of the Psalms according to the division of the Jews, for this section begins with Psalm 73 and ends with Psalm 89, and so we notice that this Psalm ends with “Amen, and Amen.”

88.12.12.en: 5- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms because it prophesies about the sufferings of Christ (vv. 50, 51), and the Psalm tells us of God's promise to David to establish his throne for ever, but the descendants of David were exposed to deposition, captivity and sufferings, and the solution was the Incarnation of Christ, who is the offspring of David who reigns for ever. By this the mercies of God appeared, for which the writer of the Psalm praises and gives thanks.

88.12.13.en: 6- There is a similarity between this Psalm and Psalm 73 in the sufferings that face the righteous, godly man and the importance of standing firm in faith.

88.12.14.en: 7- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
